blurb: How invisible radio waves carry your data, why walls and neighbours slow it down, and what WiFi 6 and 7 really changed.

cards.title: WiFi is just very clever radio

steps.p: Your router and phone both contain radios. They swap data by sending radio waves, the same kind of energy as FM radio, just at much higher frequencies.
A plain wave carries nothing. Data is added by rapidly changing the wave's strength and timing; the receiver reads those changes back as 0s and 1s.
The router turns radio into wired signals and back. It links your devices to each other and, through your modem, to the internet.

cards.aside: WiFi only covers the last few metres. Everything beyond your router travels through cables and fibre.

cards.q: Which radio frequency bands does home WiFi use?
cards.why: 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz. These are unlicensed bands anyone may use at low power. Higher frequencies carry more data but fade faster through walls.

cards.title: "Wi-Fi" doesn't stand for anything. "Wireless Fidelity" was invented afterwards.
cards.detail: A branding firm coined the name in 1999 because "IEEE 802.11b Direct Sequence" wasn't catchy. The "Wireless Fidelity" tagline was added later and soon dropped.

cards.statement: If your WiFi signal shows full bars, your internet connection must be fast.
cards.why: False. Bars only measure the radio link between device and router. The internet connection behind the router, or a crowded channel, can still be the bottleneck.

cards.q: Your laptop sends a photo to a printer in the same room over WiFi. Which path does it usually take?
cards.why: Via the router. On a normal home network, devices talk through the router (the access point). The data never needs to leave your home.

cards.statement: WiFi and microwave ovens use roughly the same radio frequency.
cards.why: True. Microwave ovens run near 2.45 GHz, inside WiFi's 2.4 GHz band. Their shielding leaks a little, which is why a running microwave can slow nearby 2.4 GHz WiFi.

cards.title: Packing bits into a wave

steps.p: WiFi tweaks a wave's strength and phase (where it is in its cycle) into one of many set patterns. More patterns per symbol means more bits sent each time.
OFDM splits a channel into many narrow sub-channels sent side by side. If interference hits a few, the rest still get through.
On one channel, devices mostly take turns. Each listens first, waits if the air is busy, then sends. That's called CSMA/CA.

cards.aside: Cramming in more patterns only works when the signal is clean. Far from the router, devices fall back to simpler, slower patterns.

cards.q: WiFi 6 can use 1024-QAM, with 1,024 possible signal patterns. How many bits does each symbol carry?
cards.why: 10 bits. 2¹⁰ = 1,024, so picking one of 1,024 patterns encodes 10 bits. WiFi 7's 4096-QAM carries 12 bits per symbol.

cards.statement: Two laptops on the same WiFi channel can transmit whenever they like without affecting each other.
cards.why: False. Overlapping transmissions on one channel garble each other. Devices listen before talking and back off, so the channel's capacity is shared, not multiplied.

cards.title: Your router shouts its network name about ten times every second.
cards.detail: These "beacon" messages, sent roughly every 0.1 seconds by default, announce the network name and settings. That's how your phone lists nearby networks without connecting.

cards.q: What does MIMO, a feature of modern routers with several antennas, let them do?
options: Send separate data streams at once over the same channel
Connect to the internet without a modem
cards.why: Parallel streams. Multiple-input, multiple-output uses several antennas and the way signals bounce around a room to send independent streams simultaneously, multiplying speed.

cards.q: Beamforming in a WiFi router works by…
options: Timing signals from several antennas so they add up toward your device
Physically turning the antennas to face you
Raising transmit power far above legal limits
Using a laser to aim data
cards.why: Adjusting timing. Slightly shifting each antenna's signal makes the waves reinforce in your direction and partly cancel elsewhere. Nothing moves physically.

cards.title: Three bands, different trade-offs

steps.p: Travels furthest and passes walls best, but it's crowded and narrow, with room for only about three non-overlapping channels.
Much more space, so wider and faster channels. It weakens faster through walls, so range is shorter.
Opened from around 2020 for WiFi 6E and WiFi 7. Lots of clean spectrum and very wide channels, but the shortest range of all.

cards.aside: Wider channels carry more data, like a wider road, but fewer of them fit side by side.

cards.q: In the crowded 2.4 GHz band, which channel numbers are the standard non-overlapping set?
cards.why: 1, 6 and 11. Each 2.4 GHz channel is about 20 MHz wide but channels are only 5 MHz apart, so neighbours overlap. Choosing anything else interferes with two groups.

cards.title: The original 1997 WiFi standard topped out at 2 megabits per second.
cards.detail: That's slower than a basic mobile connection today. Newer generations multiplied speeds through wider channels, denser signal patterns and multiple antennas, reaching multiple gigabits.

cards.statement: A router sold as "AX5400" will give your laptop 5,400 megabits per second.
cards.why: False. That number adds up the maximum link rates of every band combined, under ideal lab conditions. One laptop uses one band and typically sees a fraction of it.

cards.q: WiFi 6E and WiFi 7 gained much of their extra speed from…
options: Access to the 6 GHz band with wider channels
Switching from radio waves to infrared light
Using mobile phone towers as relays
cards.why: The 6 GHz band. It offers lots of uncluttered spectrum, and WiFi 7 allows channels up to 320 MHz wide, double WiFi 6's maximum.

cards.statement: Higher-frequency WiFi signals generally pass through walls less well than lower-frequency ones.
cards.why: True. Building materials tend to absorb and reflect higher frequencies more. That's why 2.4 GHz reaches the far bedroom while 6 GHz may not leave the room.

cards.title: Why WiFi slows down

steps.p: Signals fade fast with distance. Walls, metal, mirrors and water (including fish tanks and people) absorb or reflect them.
Every device and every neighbour on the same channel takes turns. One slow, distant device can hog airtime and drag everyone down.
Extra access points fill dead zones. Wired connections between them work best; wireless links between them spend some airtime relaying.

cards.aside: Newer WiFi versions schedule many devices together, which helps crowded homes more than raw top speed.

cards.title: A perfectly usable WiFi signal can arrive at less than a billionth of a watt.
cards.detail: Signal strength is measured in dBm. A decent reading of −70 dBm equals 0.0000000001 watts. Receivers are extraordinarily sensitive at picking such faint signals out of noise.

cards.q: Where is the best place for a home router?
options: Central and raised, in the open
Inside a cupboard to keep it tidy
On the floor behind the TV
In a corner next to the microwave
cards.why: Central and high. Signals spread outward, so a central, elevated spot covers the home evenly. Cupboards, metal and electronics absorb or interfere with the waves.

cards.statement: Your WiFi password encrypts your data all the way to the websites you visit.
cards.why: False. WiFi encryption (WPA2 or WPA3) only protects the radio hop to the router. Protection beyond that comes from HTTPS, the padlock in your browser.

cards.q: Which WiFi security setting should you avoid because it can be cracked in minutes?
cards.why: WEP. The original late-1990s scheme has deep design flaws and free tools break it quickly. Use WPA3, or WPA2 with a long password if older devices need it.

cards.title: Find your WiFi's weak spots
cards.body: Run a speed test next to the router, then in your worst room. A big drop means placement or walls are the problem, not your internet plan.
cards.challenge: Test speed in three rooms today and move the router toward the slowest one if you can.
